questions.question: Differentiate between natural and man-made aquatic pollution. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Differentiate between natural and man-made aquatic pollution.
  • Natural aquatic pollution : Occurs from natural processes like soil
  • erosion, volcanic eruptions, and decaying vegetation , Mostly
  • sediments, organic matter, and minerals.
  • Often occasional or seasonal , Usually limited and part of natural
  • ecosystem cycles.
  • Man-made aquatic pollution : Caused by human activities such as
  • industrial discharge, agricultural runoff, and sewage disposal,
  • Chemicals, heavy metals, pesticides, fertilizers, plastics, and
  • pathogens, Continuous or frequent, depending on human activity ,
  • Often severe, persistent, and harmful to aquatic life and human
  • health

questions.question: Why is bioremediation considered a natural process? / [CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• Why is bioremediation considered a natural process?
  • Bioremediation is considered a natural process because it uses
  • living organisms—such as bacteria, fungi, and plants—to break
  • down, degrade, or transform pollutants in the environment into less
  • harmful substances. The process mimics natural decomposition and
  • metabolic activities that occur in ecosystems, accelerating the self-
  • purification of soil and water without introducing synthetic
  • chemicals.

questions.question: Define Chemical Oxygen Demand (COD) and explain why it is important. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Define Chemical Oxygen Demand (COD) and explain why it is
  • important.
  • Chemical Oxygen Demand (COD) is the amount of oxygen required
  • to chemically oxidize the organic and inorganic matter present in a
  • water sample using a strong chemical oxidant, usually potassium
  • dichromate, under acidic conditions. It is expressed in milligrams of
  • oxygen per liter (mg/L).
  • Importance of COD: Measures pollution level, Quick assessment,
  • Industrial monitoring, Ecosystem health

questions.question: Write any two limitations of water quality index / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain how heavy metals enter aquatic ecosystem.
  • Industrial discharge – Effluents from mining, metal processing,
  • battery manufacturing, and electroplating industries release metals
  • like lead, mercury, cadmium, and chromium into water bodies.
  • Agricultural runoff – Use of pesticides, fertilizers, and sewage sludge
  • containing metals contributes to contamination.
  • Urban runoff and sewage – Waste from households, plumbing, and
  • urban areas carries metals such as copper, zinc, and nickel into
  • rivers and lakes.
  • Atmospheric deposition – Metals from air pollution (e.g., from
  • burning coal or smelting) settle on water surfaces or are washed
  • down by rain.
  • Natural sources – Weathering of rocks and volcanic activity can
  • release small amounts of metals into aquatic environments.

questions.question: Explain any five disadvantages of phytoremediation / [CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain any five disadvantages of phytoremediation
  • Slow process – Phytoremediation can take months or years to clean
  • up contaminated sites, making it unsuitable for urgent remediation.
  • Limited to shallow contamination – Plant roots can only reach
  • surface or near-surface pollutants, leaving deeper contaminants
  • untreated.
  • Species-specific – Only certain plants can tolerate or accumulate
  • specific pollutants, limiting its applicability.
  • Risk of contaminant transfer – Contaminants can enter the food
  • chain if animals eat the plants used for remediation.
  • Ineffective for all pollutants – It may not remove highly toxic,
  • volatile, or persistent chemicals efficiently, such as some heavy
  • metals or synthetic organics.

questions.question: Explain how sewage reduces the dissolved oxygen content of water. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain how sewage reduces the dissolved oxygen content of
  • water.
  • Introduction of organic matter – Sewage contains high amounts of
  • organic waste, such as food residues, fecal matter, and detergents.
  • Microbial decomposition – Aerobic bacteria in water break down this
  • organic matter, consuming large amounts of dissolved oxygen in the
  • process.
  • Oxygen depletion – As oxygen is used up for decomposition, DO
  • levels drop, creating hypoxic (low-oxygen) conditions.
  • Impact on aquatic life – Low oxygen can kill fish, invertebrates, and
  • other sensitive organisms, disrupting the ecosystem.
